source.title: American Football Position Does Not Influence Symmetry in Joint Power During High-Speed Running

paper.citation: Mokha M, Crisanti A, Bommarito P. American Football Position Does Not Influence Symmetry in Joint Power During High-Speed Running. Research in Strength and Performance. 2026;6(1).
paper.abstract: Sixty-eight draft-eligible American football players (Big, Big-skill and Skill groups) ran once on an instrumented treadmill at 6.4 m/s with motion capture. Joint power at the ankle, knee and hip was computed by inverse dynamics. Interlimb symmetry was measured with an asymmetry index, and groups were compared with Kruskal-Wallis tests. Position groups did not differ in asymmetry for any joint or power direction. Asymmetry differed by joint, and the ankle was the most symmetrical joint while the knee was the least symmetrical.
paper.tldr: In one high-speed running trial, player position did not change how evenly joint power was shared between the legs. Asymmetry was larger at the knee than at the ankle. The result is a no-difference finding in 18 to 26 players per group, so small differences cannot be ruled out.
paper.methods: Sixty-eight players from a pre-draft training camp, grouped as Big (n = 18), Big-skill (n = 24) and Skill (n = 26), ran one 5 s trial at their preferred maximum speed on an instrumented split-belt treadmill (mean speed 6.4 m/s). Joint power was computed by inverse dynamics and expressed as positive and negative percentages of total limb power. The asymmetry index compared left and right values. Groups were compared with Kruskal-Wallis tests and Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc tests (alpha = 0.017), with the Methods naming the Kruskal-Wallis test and the Results reporting F statistics.
paper.findings: No significant difference in asymmetry between position groups for any joint or power direction (positive power: ankle p = .868, knee p = .082, hip p = .846; negative power: ankle p = .222, knee p = .181, hip p = .496). Asymmetry did differ by joint. For positive power the knee was highest (31.9 ± 24.5%), then hip (18.1 ± 28.9%), then ankle (9.6 ± 6.9%). For negative power the ankle was lowest (11.9 ± 14.1%) and the knee (22.4 ± 16.6%) and hip (22.8 ± 19.5%) were similar. The authors' hypothesis that the ankle would be most symmetrical was supported. The reported test statistics do not match the named Kruskal-Wallis test, so they should be checked against the published PDF before quoting.
paper.limitations: One session in the weeks after the collegiate season. One running trial per player. Limb dominance, injury history and laterality were not assessed. Only steady treadmill running was tested. The authors describe the study as exploratory and cite clinical asymmetry thresholds without an injury outcome. The title's 'does not influence' is stronger than the data allow, because the groups were small and no sample-size calculation is printed.
paper.practicalImplications: Do not assume that position alone sets a player's limb asymmetry in running power. Read each athlete's asymmetry against that athlete's own history. The knee showed the largest asymmetry in this sample, so it may be worth tracking alongside the ankle, but this study cannot show that it predicts injury.
paper.athleteDev: The group values can give a rough sense of what is typical for highly trained football players in one running test. They do not show how asymmetry changes over a training year.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It has no injury or return-to-play outcome, and the clinical thresholds the authors cite cannot be tested with these data.
